essays.question: Many feel that advertising harms traditional values. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Advertisements now appear on screens, streets and phones, and many feel that advertising harms traditional values. I agree to some extent, since advertising can weaken traditional values by promoting consumption, although it is not the only influence on society.

To begin with, advertising can weaken traditional values. Adverts that link happiness to buying and that use foreign lifestyles can displace modest habits and family customs. A campaign that shows a perfect life as one with the latest phone and fashionable clothes, for example, may persuade young people that status matters more than modesty or respect for elders. Traditional values such as saving money, repairing old things and sharing with relatives can seem old-fashioned when advertisers present constant consumption as normal. Children who grow up with such messages often put pressure on their parents to buy brands, which strains family budgets and relationships.

However, advertising is not the only force that changes values, and it can sometimes support them. Some campaigns celebrate local festivals, family reunions and national crafts, and they make traditions visible to a wide audience. A holiday advert that shows several generations eating together, for example, reminds viewers of the importance of family. Values also change through education, migration, travel and the internet, so that blaming advertising alone is unfair. Governments can reduce the harm by setting standards on honesty and by encouraging adverts which respect local culture, while families and schools teach critical thinking about commercial messages.

In conclusion, I agree to some extent that advertising harms traditional values, particularly by encouraging materialism, but its influence should not be exaggerated.

essays.question: To what extent do you agree or disagree that social media causes loneliness?

versions.text:
Millions of people check their phones many times a day to see messages and photographs from friends, and some claim that social media causes loneliness. I agree to a limited extent, since social media can increase loneliness when it replaces real contact, but it also connects isolated people.

To begin with, social media can increase loneliness when it replaces face-to-face contact. Hours of scrolling reduce time spent with real friends and invite unhealthy comparison. A teenager who spends every evening looking at pictures of friends at parties, for example, may feel excluded and conclude that her own life is dull. Fear of missing out is a common feeling, and counting likes can make users anxious about their popularity. Online friendships are often shallow, since people share only the best moments and rarely talk about real worries, so that users may have hundreds of contacts yet nobody to confide in. Several studies have linked heavy use with depression and lower life satisfaction.

However, social media can also reduce isolation. Online groups help the housebound, migrants and people with rare interests to find friends. An elderly woman who cannot leave her flat, for example, can chat with grandchildren on video and join a discussion group for her hobbies. People who live abroad can stay in touch with their families, and those who are shy may find it easier to start conversations online and then meet in person. The effect therefore depends on how it is used: as a complement to real relationships, social media can be helpful, while as a substitute it is harmful. Setting limits on screen time and prioritising real meetings can protect users.

In conclusion, social media causes loneliness only to a limited extent, and its effect depends on how people use it.

essays.question: Many feel that celebrities have a negative influence on young people. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Young people follow singers, footballers and film stars on screens every day, and many feel that celebrities have a negative influence on them. I agree to some extent, since some celebrities set a poor example, although others have a very positive influence.

To begin with, celebrities can set a negative example for young fans. Young people imitate stars who display luxury, extreme diets or reckless behaviour. A teenager who sees an idol spend huge sums on fashion and cars, for example, may feel that happiness depends on money and may try to copy that lifestyle. Pictures of unnaturally thin models and edited bodies can lead to dissatisfaction with appearance and eating problems, and scandals involving drugs, alcohol or violence may make such behaviour seem acceptable. Because fans often look up to their idols, they may defend their actions or follow their habits without thinking about the consequences. Many stars also promote products in return for payment, which encourages young people to buy things they do not need.

However, many celebrities inspire positive habits. Athletes and artists who work hard, give to charity or speak about mental health encourage young people to do the same. A footballer who grew up in poverty and now funds schools, for example, shows what discipline and generosity can achieve. Musicians who talk openly about their own struggles help fans to feel less alone, and actors who support environmental campaigns raise awareness among their followers. The influence therefore depends on which role models are promoted. Parents and teachers can help by discussing the lives of public figures critically and by drawing attention to those who offer genuine examples.

In conclusion, I agree to some extent that celebrities can influence young people negatively, but the overall effect depends on the example that they set.

essays.question: Many feel that traditional media is less trustworthy than online sources. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Readers once relied on newspapers and television bulletins, but today many get their information from websites and social networks, and many feel that traditional media is less trustworthy than online sources. I disagree with this view, since traditional media usually checks facts and carries legal responsibility, although it is not perfect.

To begin with, traditional media is usually more reliable than online sources. Editors verify stories and can be held accountable, while anyone can post online without checking. A national newspaper that publishes a false claim, for example, risks legal action and loss of reputation, so reporters need two or more sources before printing. Professional journalists are trained in ethics, and newsrooms have procedures for corrections. Many online sources, in contrast, are anonymous, funded by advertising that rewards shocking headlines, or created to spread a political message. Fake stories travel faster than corrections on social platforms, and users often share content without reading it.

However, traditional media is not free from faults. It can be biased by owners or political leanings, it may be slow to react to events, and it sometimes ignores topics that do not interest its main audience. Online sources have advantages: they are fast, offer diverse views and allow ordinary people to record events that official media overlook. Some independent websites and blogs provide excellent analysis. Readers should therefore compare several sources, check who is responsible for a report and look for evidence. Schools can teach media literacy so that young people learn to distinguish reliable from unreliable information.

In conclusion, I disagree that traditional media is less trustworthy than online sources, although readers should always use several sources and think critically.

essays.question: Many feel that photos and posts on social media are misleading. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
A holiday photograph with perfect light, a smiling family and a spotless home appears in thousands of feeds every day, and many feel that photos and posts on social media are misleading. I agree with this view, since people edit and select what they show, although some posts are honest.

To begin with, photos and posts on social media are often misleading because people edit and select what they show. Filters, editing and carefully chosen moments create flawless images of life. A young woman who spends an hour taking fifty pictures before posting the best one, for example, may use filters to change her skin and shape, so that the result differs greatly from reality. People share holidays, promotions and celebrations, but rarely mention arguments, failures and ordinary days. Influencers may also be paid to praise products without admitting that they have not used them, and some staged scenes are presented as spontaneous.

Furthermore, these images affect viewers. Those who see only perfect lives compare themselves unfairly and feel dissatisfied with their own appearance, income or relationships. Teenagers are especially vulnerable, since they are still forming their identity, and research has linked heavy use with anxiety and low self-esteem. However, not all posts are dishonest, and many people use the platforms to share real experiences, news and creative work. Media literacy and honest labelling reduce the harm. Schools can teach students how images are edited, platforms can require labels on altered or sponsored photographs, and users can remind themselves that online lives are selected highlights.

In conclusion, I agree that many photos and posts on social media are misleading, but education and clear labelling can help people to view them more critically.

essays.question: To what extent do you agree or disagree that books are better than films?

versions.text:
Every year, popular novels are turned into films, and people often debate which form is better, so that the statement that books are better than films raises a lively question. I agree to a large extent, although films have strengths of their own.

To begin with, books develop imagination and language more deeply. Reading requires readers to picture scenes, builds vocabulary and allows detailed ideas. A reader of a long novel, for example, imagines the faces, voices and places in his own way, and meets sentences and words that he would rarely hear in conversation. Books allow access to the inner thoughts of characters, which films can only suggest, and they can explore complicated arguments, history and science in great depth. Reading also improves concentration and writing skills, and it is a portable and cheap hobby that can be enjoyed anywhere. Studies suggest that regular readers have larger vocabularies and better understanding of others.

However, films give vivid and emotional experiences quickly. They combine images, music and acting to deliver a story in two hours, which suits people who have little time. A film adaptation of a classic, for example, can introduce a story to those who would never open the book, and spectacular scenes such as battles or landscapes are more powerful on screen. Films can also be watched with friends and discussed afterwards. Therefore, each form has its strengths, and the best choice depends on purpose: for deep learning, language and reflection, books are superior, while for entertainment and shared experience, films are often more convenient.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that books are better than films, but both have an important place in culture.

essays.question: Many feel that adverts target children inappropriately. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Cartoon characters, free toys and bright colours fill many programmes and websites that children watch, and many feel that adverts target children inappropriately. I agree with this view, since young children cannot judge persuasion, although some advertising can be harmless.

To begin with, advertising aimed at children is unfair because they cannot judge persuasion. Young children do not understand that adverts sell, so cartoon characters and games lead them to demand toys and sugary snacks. A six-year-old who sees a favourite character on a cereal box, for example, believes that the product is special and will repeat the request until her parents agree. Children do not have the experience to evaluate claims or to resist pressure, and psychologists say that before the age of eight they take messages at face value. Advertisers also use tricks such as competitions, collectable items and websites that blend games with promotions to make children want the brand.

Furthermore, such advertising has harmful effects. It pressures parents who must refuse again and again, and it encourages materialism and unhealthy habits, because many adverts promote sweets, fast food and expensive toys. Children who cannot have the latest fashion may feel left out, which damages their self-esteem. However, not all advertising to children is harmful, and some promotes books, sports or educational games. Strict rules are nevertheless justified: governments can ban manipulative techniques, limit adverts during children's programmes, require clear labelling of promotions and restrict the promotion of unhealthy food. Parents and schools should also teach children how advertising works.

In conclusion, I agree that adverts target children inappropriately, and stricter regulation would protect them.

essays.question: Some believe that governments should limit advertising of unhealthy food. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Posters for burgers, sweets and fizzy drinks surround children on screens and streets, and some believe that governments should limit advertising of unhealthy food. I agree to a large extent, since such advertising shapes children's choices and fuels obesity, although education must go with it.

To begin with, governments should restrict advertising of unhealthy food because it shapes children's choices. Repeated adverts for sweets and fast food make them attractive and normal. A child who sees a burger advertised during every cartoon, for example, will ask for it, and food companies spend huge sums on this because it works. Obesity and type two diabetes are rising rapidly among young people, which costs health services billions and shortens lives. Experiments show that children who watch such adverts eat more snacks immediately afterwards. Limiting broadcast times and locations reduces demand, and countries that have banned such advertising before nine in the evening or near schools have recorded reductions in the purchase of unhealthy products.

However, advertising limits alone are not sufficient, and they raise questions about freedom of trade. Companies argue that their products are legal and that consumers are responsible for their own choices. Parents also have a role in shaping habits at home. Education should therefore accompany restrictions: schools can teach nutrition and cooking, labelling can show sugar and fat clearly, and healthy food should be made cheaper and easier to find. Taxes on sugary drinks have also encouraged manufacturers to reduce sugar. When these measures are combined, public health costs fall and children grow up with better habits.

In conclusion, I agree that governments should limit the advertising of unhealthy food, as long as this is part of a wider strategy for healthy living.

essays.question: To what extent should governments regulate social media content? Give reasons for your answer.

versions.text:
Posts, videos and comments spread across social platforms in seconds, and the question is to what extent governments should regulate social media content. I believe that governments should regulate illegal and harmful content, but they should avoid censoring legitimate opinion.

To begin with, governments should regulate content that is clearly illegal or harmful. Platforms spread hate speech, threats and content harmful to children, so laws can demand quick removal. A video that encourages violence against a minority group, for example, can lead to real attacks if it is shared widely, and companies may not act unless they face penalties. Material such as child abuse images, terrorist propaganda and fraud is already illegal offline, and there is no reason why it should be tolerated online. Governments can also require platforms to protect young users, to publish reports on the removal of harmful posts and to give users ways to complain. Without regulation, companies tend to put profit before safety.

However, vague or excessive rules allow officials to silence critics, and freedom of expression is a basic right. A law that bans posts that insult the government, for example, could be used to punish journalists and opponents. Opinions that are unpopular or offensive to some people are not necessarily harmful, and open debate helps societies to find the truth. Clear, narrow rules, with independent oversight and the right to appeal, protect both safety and freedom. Platforms should also be transparent about how their algorithms and moderation work. Cooperation between governments, companies and civil society is more effective than control by the state alone.

In conclusion, governments should regulate social media content to a moderate extent, concentrating on illegal and clearly harmful material while protecting freedom of speech.

essays.question: Many people think that social networks increase cyberbullying. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
A cruel message, a humiliating photograph or a false rumour can reach a whole school within minutes, and many people think that social networks increase cyberbullying. I agree with this view, since abuse can be anonymous, constant and public, although bullying also exists offline.

To begin with, social networks increase cyberbullying because abuse can be anonymous, constant and public. Bullies can reach victims at any hour and share insults with a large audience, so harm spreads quickly and is hard to escape. A girl who is mocked by classmates in a group chat, for example, may receive messages late at night in her own bedroom, where she once felt safe. Offensive comments and edited pictures can be copied and shared endlessly, and they can remain online for years. Anonymous accounts remove the fear of being identified, which makes some people far crueller than they would be in person, and observers often join in without thinking.

Furthermore, the consequences can be severe. Victims often suffer anxiety, depression and loss of sleep, perform worse at school and, in tragic cases, harm themselves. However, bullying existed long before the internet, and some of it still takes place in classrooms and playgrounds. Social networks have not created cruelty; they have given it new tools and a larger audience. Platforms, schools and parents must therefore act together. Platforms should make it easy to report abuse, remove harmful posts quickly and block repeat offenders, schools should teach students how to behave online and how to support victims, and parents should talk openly with their children and keep an eye on warning signs.

In conclusion, I agree that social networks increase cyberbullying, and effective protection requires cooperation between technology companies, schools and families.

Agree; cần hợp tác.

essays.question: Discuss the role of documentaries in educating the public.

versions.text:
Documentaries about nature, history and social problems attract millions of viewers on television and streaming platforms, and this essay will discuss the role of documentaries in educating the public, focusing on how they present evidence and how they raise awareness.

To begin with, documentaries educate the public by showing real events and complex issues in an accessible way. Film combines evidence, interviews and images that make topics such as climate or history memorable. A viewer who watches a documentary about plastic in the oceans, for example, sees turtles caught in nets and beaches covered in rubbish, which is far more powerful than reading a statistic. Experts explain difficult ideas in plain language, and animation, maps and archive footage make them easier to grasp. People who would never open a scientific textbook may therefore learn about medicine, space or economics in an evening.

Furthermore, documentaries raise awareness and encourage action. They bring attention to problems that are neglected in the news, such as modern slavery, and they can change opinions and policies. Several films about food production have led consumers to change their habits and governments to tighten rules. Schools use documentaries to bring lessons to life, and they allow viewers to visit places and cultures they could never see. However, directors may present a one-sided view or simplify, and viewers should not accept every claim without question. Documentaries are best treated as a starting point for further reading, discussion and independent thinking.

In conclusion, documentaries play an important role in educating the public by presenting evidence vividly and drawing attention to important issues, provided that viewers remain critical.

essays.question: Many feel that streaming services have reduced box office sales. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Many people now watch new films on a laptop or television a few weeks after release, and many feel that streaming services have reduced box office sales. I agree to a large extent, since streaming has reduced cinema attendance for ordinary films, although big releases still fill theatres.

To begin with, streaming has reduced cinema attendance for ordinary films. Viewers can watch a wide choice at home for a monthly fee. A family of four who would pay a large sum for tickets, snacks and parking, for example, can instead watch several films at home for a fraction of the cost, and they can pause, rewind and choose the time. Studios that launch their own platforms sometimes release films online on the same day as in cinemas, which gives people little reason to go out. Medium-budget dramas and comedies, which once earned steady revenue, have suffered most, and many small cinemas have closed.

However, the large screen, sound and shared atmosphere of cinemas keep attracting audiences to major films. Spectacular action films, superhero stories and animated features regularly earn record sums, because many people want an experience that a home cannot match. A group of friends who see a new blockbuster together, for example, enjoy the excitement of reacting with a crowd. Other factors have also reduced sales, including rising ticket prices, the pandemic and competition from games and social media, so streaming is not the only cause. Cinemas can respond by offering comfortable seats, special screenings and events, which makes a visit more than just watching a film.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that streaming has reduced box office sales, particularly for modest films, but cinemas will survive by offering experiences that homes cannot.

essays.question: Many people think that reality TV encourages bad behaviour. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Programmes in which strangers share a house or compete for a prize are popular around the world, and many people think that reality television encourages bad behaviour. I agree to a large extent, since such shows often reward conflict and shallow fame, although a few have positive aspects.

To begin with, reality television often rewards conflict and shallow fame, which can encourage poor behaviour. Producers choose arguments, insults and scandals that attract viewers, so young audiences may imitate rudeness and think fame matters more than effort. A contestant who shouts at others and receives millions of views, for example, may become a celebrity, which sends the message that aggression is a path to success. Editing creates villains and exaggerates quarrels, and participants are encouraged to gossip, lie and betray each other in order to win. Viewers who watch such behaviour week after week may come to see it as normal and may copy the language and attitudes in their own schools and offices.

However, not all reality shows are harmful, and a few teach skills or kindness. Cooking and singing competitions, for example, show contestants who practise for years and support each other, and home renovation programmes demonstrate practical skills. Some documentaries in the genre follow families through difficult times and increase understanding of other people. The influence therefore depends on the programme and on the viewer. Parents should talk with children about what they watch, and broadcasters should avoid deliberately provoking conflict or humiliating participants. Viewers need critical awareness and should remember that what they see has been edited for entertainment.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that reality television encourages bad behaviour, but its effect depends on the programme and on how critically it is watched.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: truyền hình thực tế khuyến khích hành vi xấu — largely agree

Largely agree; phụ thuộc chương trình và cách xem.

essays.question: Many feel that fake news spreads too easily online. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
A shocking headline can be shared with thousands of people before anyone checks whether it is true, and many feel that fake news spreads too easily online. I agree with this view, since sharing is instant and emotional stories travel fastest, although some measures can limit the problem.

To begin with, fake news spreads too easily because sharing is instant and emotional stories travel fastest. Users forward posts without checking, algorithms promote shocking content, and false stories can reach millions before corrections appear. A false report about a medicine that cures a disease, for example, may be shared by worried relatives who believe they are helping, and some may then refuse proper treatment. Studies show that untrue stories are more likely to be shared than accurate ones because they are surprising and provoke anger or fear. Anyone can create a convincing website or video using cheap tools, and fake accounts can make a story look popular.

Furthermore, the consequences are serious. False claims about vaccines have reduced immunisation, rumours during elections influence voters and invented stories about minorities have caused violence. However, the situation is not hopeless. Verification tools, fact-checking organisations and labels on disputed posts help users to identify misleading content, and platforms can reduce the reach of repeated offenders. Media education is also vital: schools should teach students to check sources, look for evidence and think before sharing. When these steps are combined with fair laws against deliberate disinformation, fake news will find it harder to spread.

In conclusion, I agree that fake news spreads too easily online, and responsibility is shared by platforms, governments, schools and ordinary users.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: tin giả lan quá dễ — agree

plan.think: Mở bài nêu tiêu đề gây sốc chia sẻ trước khi kiểm; agree.

Chia sẻ tức thì, chuyện cảm xúc lan nhanh nhất: người dùng chuyển tiếp không kiểm, thuật toán đẩy nội dung gây sốc; ví dụ tin sai về thuốc chữa bệnh được người thân lo lắng chia sẻ, có người từ chối điều trị; nghiên cứu: chuyện sai dễ chia sẻ hơn vì bất ngờ, gây giận, sợ; công cụ rẻ tạo trang web, video thuyết phục, tài khoản giả tạo cảm giác phổ biến.

Trách nhiệm chung.

essays.question: To what extent do you agree or disagree that advertising should be banned from children’s programs?

versions.text:
Children watch cartoons and educational programmes for hours every week, and some people think that advertising should be banned from children's programmes. I agree to a large extent, since such a ban would protect young viewers, although the television industry will need alternative funding.

To begin with, advertising should be banned from children's programmes because it exploits young viewers. Children cannot judge persuasion, and adverts fuel pester power, which means that they keep demanding products from their parents. A child who sees a toy advertised between two cartoons, for example, believes that she needs it, and a parent who refuses may face tears and arguments. Many adverts promote sugary snacks and expensive items, which encourages unhealthy habits and materialism. Some countries, including Sweden and Norway, have banned or strictly limited advertising aimed at children, and they have not seen the quality of programmes decline. A programme that is free of commercial breaks allows children to concentrate on the story and the lesson.

However, channels rely on advertising income, so alternative funding is needed. If commercial channels lose income, they may reduce the quality or quantity of children's programmes, which would harm young viewers. Public funding, subsidies for educational content or limited sponsorship that does not promote products can fill the gap. In addition, children now watch many videos online, where a ban on television alone would have little effect, so rules should cover digital platforms too. Parents can also teach children how advertising works. Quality television for children can survive without ads, as public broadcasters have shown for decades.

In conclusion, I agree that advertising should be banned from children's programmes, provided that governments find other sources of funding.

grade.summary: Bài viết đạt chất lượng tốt, cấu trúc mạch lạc và từ vựng phong phú về chủ đề quảng cáo cho trẻ em. Để đạt điểm cao hơn ở tiêu chí Coherence & Cohesion, bạn cần phân tách đoạn thân bài thứ hai thành các đoạn nhỏ hơn để làm rõ từng ý phụ.
weaknesses: Đoạn thân bài thứ hai bị quá tải với nhiều ý tưởng khác nhau (nguồn vốn, YouTube/online, vai trò phụ huynh) nên cần tách nhỏ.
Sự liên kết giữa các câu đôi chỗ có thể mượt mà hơn để tránh cảm giác liệt kê ý.

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết trả lời tốt câu hỏi theo hướng đồng ý một phần (đồng ý nhưng có điều kiện). Lập luận phát triển rõ ràng với các ví dụ thực tế như Thụy Điển và Na Uy, đồng thời xem xét cả mặt trái về nguồn vốn.
feedback.coherenceCohesion: Bố cục bài viết mạch lạc với phần mở bài, thân bài và kết luận rõ ràng. Tuy nhiên, đoạn thân bài thứ hai khá dài và chứa quá nhiều ý khác nhau (nguồn vốn, nền tảng trực tuyến, vai trò của phụ huynh), làm giảm tính liên kết.
feedback.lexicalResource: Sử dụng từ vựng phong phú, tự nhiên và đúng chủ đề như 'exploit young viewers', 'pester power', 'materialism', 'alternative funding'. Không có lỗi chính tả đáng kể nào.
feedback.grammar: Cấu trúc ngữ pháp đa dạng, sử dụng linh hoạt câu phức và các mệnh đề quan hệ. Đội ngũ kiểm tra ghi nhận độ chính xác cao về mặt ngữ pháp.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: cấm quảng cáo trong chương trình trẻ em — largely agree

plan.think: Mở bài nêu trẻ xem hoạt hình, chương trình giáo dục hàng giờ; largely agree.

Quảng cáo khai thác người xem trẻ: trẻ không phán đoán được thuyết phục, thúc ép cha mẹ; ví dụ trẻ thấy đồ chơi giữa hai phim hoạt hình tin cần có, cha mẹ từ chối bị khóc, cãi; quảng cáo kẹo, đồ đắt khuyến khích thói quen xấu, vật chất; Thuỵ Điển, Na Uy cấm hoặc hạn chế mà chất lượng không giảm; chương trình không quảng cáo tập trung.

Kênh phụ thuộc quảng cáo: mất thu nhập giảm chất lượng; tài trợ công, trợ cấp nội dung giáo dục, tài trợ hạn chế không quảng bá sản phẩm; trẻ xem video trực tuyến nên quy tắc cần phủ nền tảng số; cha mẹ dạy; đài công cho thấy có thể.
Đồng ý nếu tìm nguồn tài trợ khác.

essays.question: Some people say that advertising for unhealthy foods should be restricted. Do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Advertisements for crisps, soft drinks and fast food appear on billboards, in magazines and during popular television shows, and some people say that advertising for unhealthy foods should be restricted. I agree with this view, since such advertising shapes choices, especially those of children, and contributes to health problems.

To begin with, advertising for unhealthy foods should be restricted because it influences what people eat. Advertisers spend large sums to make sweets and fast food look exciting, and the constant exposure makes them seem normal parts of daily life. A teenager who sees a sports star drinking a sugary beverage in an advertisement, for example, may link it with success and energy. Obesity, diabetes and heart disease are increasing worldwide, and unhealthy diets are a major cause, which burdens hospitals and reduces productivity. Children are particularly vulnerable because they cannot recognise persuasion, and food preferences formed early often last for life. Limits on broadcasting times and on advertising near schools have helped to reduce the consumption of unhealthy products in some countries.

However, restrictions should be accompanied by other measures. Food companies argue that their products are legal and that individuals should decide for themselves, and a complete ban would reduce revenue for media and companies. A balanced approach would restrict the advertising of the unhealthiest products at times when children are watching, require clear nutritional information and encourage adverts for healthy alternatives. Education in schools can teach children about nutrition, and healthier food should be made affordable. Together, these steps lower the demand for junk food without removing freedom of choice.

In conclusion, I agree that advertising for unhealthy foods should be restricted, since it affects health, but restrictions should be part of a broader strategy.

grade.summary: Bài viết có bố cục tốt, lập luận rõ ràng và ngôn ngữ phong phú, đạt mức điểm khá. Tuy nhiên, việc đưa quá nhiều giải pháp ở đoạn thân bài thứ hai đã làm giảm sự tập trung vào yêu cầu chính của đề bài.
weaknesses: Đoạn thân bài thứ hai hơi lan man sang bàn về giải pháp toàn diện thay vì tập trung phân tích sâu hơn vào việc hạn chế quảng cáo.
Thiếu các ví dụ cụ thể mang tính toàn cầu hoặc số liệu để chứng minh luận điểm mạnh mẽ hơn.

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết trả lời tốt câu hỏi đề bài, thể hiện rõ quan điểm đồng tình ở cả phần mở bài, thân bài và kết bài. Tuy nhiên, đoạn thân bài thứ hai lại lạc sang bàn về các giải pháp toàn diện thay vì tập trung bảo vệ lập trường đồng tình hoặc phản biện, làm phân tán trọng tâm.
feedback.coherenceCohesion: Bố cục bài viết mạch lạc với cấu trúc 4 đoạn rõ ràng. Các liên kết từ và cụm từ chuyển ý được sử dụng tự nhiên, giúp người đọc dễ theo dõi mạch luận điểm.
feedback.lexicalResource: Vốn từ vựng phong phú, sử dụng tốt các từ liên quan đến chủ đề sức khỏe và quảng cáo như 'constant exposure', 'vulnerable', 'persuasion'. Một số cụm từ diễn đạt tự nhiên và chính xác.
feedback.grammar: Cấu trúc câu đa dạng, kết hợp linh hoạt giữa câu đơn, câu ghép và câu phức. Hầu hết các câu đều viết đúng ngữ pháp, rất ít lỗi sai sót.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: hạn chế quảng cáo đồ ăn không lành mạnh (khác #115: thiên về đối tượng chung)

plan.think: Mở bài nêu quảng cáo khoai chiên, nước ngọt, đồ ăn nhanh khắp nơi; agree.

Ảnh hưởng điều con người ăn: chi nhiều làm kẹo, đồ ăn nhanh hấp dẫn, quen thuộc; ví dụ thiếu niên thấy ngôi sao thể thao uống nước ngọt gắn với thành công, năng lượng; béo phì, tiểu đường, tim tăng, gánh nặng bệnh viện; trẻ dễ tổn thương, sở thích định hình sớm; giới hạn giờ, gần trường giảm tiêu thụ.

Công ty cho là hợp pháp, cá nhân tự quyết, cấm hoàn toàn giảm thu nhập; cách cân bằng: hạn chế sản phẩm không lành mạnh nhất khi trẻ xem, thông tin dinh dưỡng rõ, quảng cáo thay thế lành mạnh; giáo dục dinh dưỡng; đồ lành mạnh giá phải chăng; giảm cầu mà giữ tự do chọn.
Agree; nằm trong chiến lược rộng.

essays.question: Many people think that binge-watching TV has negative effects. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Streaming platforms release whole series at once, and many people watch ten episodes in a single weekend, so many people think that binge-watching TV has negative effects. I agree to a large extent when it is excessive, although occasional marathons are harmless.

To begin with, binge-watching harms health and time use when it is excessive. Hours of sitting reduce sleep and exercise and replace study or social time. A student who stays up until four in the morning to finish a series, for example, will be exhausted at lectures and may fall behind with her work. Long periods of inactivity are linked to weight gain, back pain and heart problems, and blue light from screens disturbs sleep. Researchers have also found that heavy bingers feel more lonely and more depressed than moderate viewers, partly because they may avoid friends and activities. Some people find it hard to stop, since autoplay starts the next episode automatically and the story is designed to be gripping.

However, binge-watching is not always harmful. Watching a favourite series with friends on a rainy weekend can relax and bond people, and shared programmes provide topics for conversation. Compared with stressful work, a few hours of entertainment can be a legitimate way to recover, and many programmes are educational or artistic. The effect therefore depends on moderation and planning. Viewers can set limits, turn off autoplay, take breaks to move around and avoid watching late at night before important duties. Parents can also guide children's viewing habits.

In conclusion, I agree that binge-watching has negative effects when excessive, but moderate viewing is harmless and can be enjoyable.

grade.summary: Bài viết có chất lượng tốt, cấu trúc rõ ràng và vượt qua yêu cầu tối thiểu về số lượng từ. Lập luận và ví dụ được phát triển hợp lý, tuy nhiên cần nâng cấp một số từ vựng và cấu trúc câu để đạt mức điểm cao hơn.
weaknesses: Một số diễn đạt còn mang tính liệt kê thay vì phân tích sâu hơn.
Thiếu các cấu trúc câu phức nâng cao hơn (ví dụ: đảo ngữ, mệnh đề phân từ).

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết đã trả lời trực tiếp câu hỏi theo hướng đồng ý một phần (agree to a large extent), đưa ra được cả tác hại khi lạm dụng và lợi ích khi điều độ. Lập luận rõ ràng và có ví dụ cụ thể minh họa.
feedback.coherenceCohesion: Bố cục bài viết mạch lạc với 4 đoạn rõ ràng: mở bài, thân bài 1 (tác hại), thân bài 2 (lợi ích/điều kiện), và kết bài. Các từ nối và phương tiện liên kết được sử dụng tự nhiên và hiệu quả.
feedback.lexicalResource: Vận dụng tốt các từ vựng chủ đề (binge-watching, streaming platforms, heavy bingers, inactivity, legitimate way to recover). Tuy nhiên, một số cụm từ chưa thực sự tự nhiên hoặc mang tính học thuật cao.
feedback.grammar: Cấu trúc câu đa dạng, kết hợp tốt giữa câu đơn, câu ghép và câu phức. Ngữ pháp chính xác, lỗi sai không đáng kể và không ảnh hưởng đến việc truyền đạt ý nghĩa.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: cày phim có tác động tiêu cực — largely agree

plan.think: Mở bài nêu nền tảng phát cả series, xem 10 tập một cuối tuần; largely agree khi quá mức.

Hại sức khoẻ, thời gian khi quá mức: ngồi lâu giảm ngủ, tập; ví dụ sinh viên thức đến 4 giờ sáng kiệt sức ở giảng đường, học tụt; ít vận động liên quan tăng cân, đau lưng, tim; ánh sáng xanh; cô đơn, trầm cảm; tự phát tập tiếp.

Không luôn có hại: xem với bạn thư giãn, gắn kết, chủ đề trò chuyện; so với công việc căng thẳng giải trí giúp hồi phục; chương trình giáo dục nghệ thuật; điều độ: giới hạn, tắt tự phát, nghỉ vận động, không xem muộn; cha mẹ hướng dẫn.
Tiêu cực khi quá mức; điều độ vô hại.

essays.question: Many feel that online advertising is intrusive. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Pop-up windows, videos that start automatically and adverts that seem to follow users from site to site are part of everyday browsing, and many feel that online advertising is intrusive. I agree with this view, since it interrupts and tracks users, although it pays for much free content.

To begin with, online advertising is intrusive because it interrupts and tracks users. Pop-ups, autoplay videos and personalised tracking disturb browsing and collect data. A reader who tries to follow a news article, for example, may have to close three banners, wait for an advert to end and then find that the page jumps while it loads. Companies collect information about searches, locations and purchases to target adverts, which many people find uncomfortable, especially when they see ads for something that they mentioned in a private conversation. Mobile phone users also pay for the data that adverts consume, and some adverts slow devices or contain harmful software.

However, advertising revenue keeps many websites free, and some adverts are useful. Newspapers, video platforms and search engines depend on it, and without it, readers might have to pay for subscriptions that many cannot afford. A shopper who receives an advert for a product she was looking for may actually benefit. The answer is therefore not to abolish online advertising but to make it less intrusive. Better rules and tools balance both sides: laws should require clear consent before data are collected, limit tracking, and ban the most annoying formats, while browsers and ad blockers allow users to protect themselves. Responsible advertisers who respect users can build trust.

In conclusion, I agree that online advertising is intrusive, but with proper regulation it can remain a fair way to fund content.

grade.summary: Bài viết có chất lượng tốt với bố cục rõ ràng, từ vựng phong phú và ngữ pháp vững chắc. Lập luận chặt chẽ, đưa ra được góc nhìn đa chiều về vấn đề quảng cáo trực tuyến.
weaknesses: Một số câu ghép hơi dài, nếu tinh chỉnh lại sẽ tăng thêm tính súc tích.
Ví dụ đưa ra ở phần thân bài có thể mang tính khái quát hơn nữa thay vì kể lể chi tiết.

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết trả lời rất tốt yêu cầu của đề bài, có lập trường rõ ràng và phát triển các ý chính một cách thuyết phục. Bạn đã thảo luận cả lý do tại sao quảng cáo trực tuyến mang tính xâm phạm lẫn giải pháp cân bằng vấn đề.
feedback.coherenceCohesion: Bố cục bài viết mạch lạc, chia đoạn hợp lý và có các từ nối chuyển ý tự nhiên. Trình tự từ mở bài, thân bài đến kết bài được tổ chức rất logic.
feedback.lexicalResource: Vốn từ vựng phong phú và phù hợp với chủ đề công nghệ và quảng cáo (như 'intrusive', 'autoplay videos', 'personalised tracking', 'advertising revenue'). Các cụm từ được sử dụng tự nhiên và chính xác.
feedback.grammar: Cấu trúc ngữ pháp đa dạng, sử dụng linh hoạt các câu phức và câu ghép với độ chính xác cao. Lỗi ngữ pháp rất ít và không ảnh hưởng đến việc truyền tải ý nghĩa.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: quảng cáo trực tuyến xâm phạm — agree

plan.think: Mở bài nêu pop-up, video tự phát, quảng cáo bám theo người dùng; agree.

Làm gián đoạn và theo dõi: pop-up, video tự phát, theo dõi cá nhân làm phiền, thu dữ liệu; ví dụ người đọc báo phải đóng ba biểu ngữ, chờ quảng cáo, trang nhảy khi tải; thu thập tìm kiếm, vị trí, mua sắm; quảng cáo về điều nhắc trong trò chuyện riêng; tốn dữ liệu, làm chậm, phần mềm độc hại.

Doanh thu quảng cáo giữ trang miễn phí; báo, video, công cụ tìm kiếm phụ thuộc; không có phải trả thuê bao; ví dụ người mua nhận quảng cáo sản phẩm đang tìm có lợi; giải pháp ít xâm phạm: luật yêu cầu đồng ý rõ, hạn chế theo dõi, cấm dạng phiền nhất; trình duyệt chặn quảng cáo; nhà quảng cáo tôn trọng xây niềm tin.
Agree; điều tiết hợp lý vẫn tài trợ nội dung công bằng.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on public broadcasting? Use examples.

versions.text:
Some countries fund television and radio channels through licence fees or taxes, and this essay will discuss the benefits for a country that focuses on public broadcasting, using examples from several nations.

To begin with, public broadcasting provides reliable information and cultural programmes that commercial channels may not. Funded by licence fees or taxes, it can serve minorities, schools and remote regions and keep news independent of advertisers. The British Broadcasting Corporation, for example, produces news, drama, children's programmes and educational series that are available to everyone, and its reports are widely trusted around the world. Because public channels do not depend on audience ratings alone, they can broadcast documentaries, classical music and regional languages that attract smaller audiences but add to national culture. In emergencies such as floods, they provide accurate and calm warnings and advice to the whole population.

Furthermore, public broadcasting benefits democracy and society. It offers balanced coverage of elections and political debates, which helps citizens to make informed decisions, and it brings people together through shared experiences such as sporting events and national celebrations. Schools use its programmes in lessons, and its children's channels are free of advertising. The disadvantages are the cost to taxpayers and the risk of political pressure, but strong independence rules, transparent funding and an independent board can protect against these problems. Citizens are better informed and more united in countries with strong public broadcasters, and commercial channels also gain by competing against high standards.

In conclusion, a country that focuses on public broadcasting benefits from independent information, rich culture and a more informed society.

grade.summary: Bài viết có cấu trúc tốt, ngữ pháp vững vàng và từ vựng phong phú, đạt mức điểm khá giỏi. Để cải thiện lên band cao hơn, bạn cần tập trung hoàn toàn vào yêu cầu của đề bài và tinh chỉnh một số lỗi dùng từ, cấu trúc câu.
weaknesses: Đưa phần nhược điểm vào đoạn 2 trong khi đề bài chỉ hỏi về lợi ích (benefits), dễ làm loãng trọng tâm.
Một số diễn đạt còn mang tính liệt kê thay vì phân tích sâu sắc.
Thiếu các cấu trúc câu đảo ngữ hoặc mệnh đề phân từ nâng cao.

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết đã trả lời tốt câu hỏi về lợi ích của phát thanh truyền hình công cộng, có đưa ra ví dụ thực tế (BBC). Tuy nhiên, đoạn thân bài thứ hai có đề cập sơ qua đến nhược điểm nhưng chưa phân tích sâu do đề bài chỉ hỏi về 'benefits', phần này có thể làm lệch trọng tâm nếu không khéo léo.
feedback.coherenceCohesion: Bố cục bài viết rõ ràng với phần mở bài, thân bài và kết luận mạch lạc. Các câu liên kết tốt, sử dụng các từ chuyển ý hiệu quả như 'To begin with', 'Furthermore', và 'In conclusion'.
feedback.lexicalResource: Sử dụng từ vựng phong phú, tự nhiên và phù hợp với chủ đề truyền thông (reliable information, cultural programmes, audience ratings, balanced coverage). Tuy nhiên, thiếu một vài cụm từ học thuật nâng cao hơn (band 8+).
feedback.grammar: Cấu trúc câu đa dạng, từ câu đơn đến câu phức đều được kiểm soát tốt và ít lỗi ngữ pháp. Các thì và sự hòa hợp giữa chủ ngữ và động từ được sử dụng chính xác.

analysis.type_vi: A/D (benefits): phát thanh truyền hình công — ví dụ BBC

plan.think: Mở bài nêu tài trợ bằng phí cấp phép hoặc thuế; lợi ích với ví dụ.

Thông tin đáng tin, chương trình văn hoá thương mại bỏ qua: phục vụ thiểu số, trường, vùng xa, tin độc lập với nhà quảng cáo; ví dụ BBC tin, kịch, trẻ em, giáo dục cho mọi người, tin cậy toàn cầu; không phụ thuộc rating nên có tài liệu, nhạc cổ điển, ngôn ngữ vùng; khẩn cấp lũ cảnh báo chính xác.

Lợi cho dân chủ và xã hội: bầu cử cân bằng, quyết định sáng suốt; gắn kết qua sự kiện thể thao, lễ quốc gia; trường dùng; kênh trẻ em không quảng cáo; nhược: chi phí thuế, áp lực chính trị; quy tắc độc lập, tài trợ minh bạch, hội đồng độc lập; kênh thương mại cạnh tranh chuẩn cao.
Thông tin độc lập, văn hoá, xã hội hiểu biết.

essays.question: Many feel that celebrity endorsements are misleading. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
When a famous actor smiles from a billboard while holding a perfume bottle or a bank card, viewers may assume that the star really uses it, and many feel that celebrity endorsements are misleading. I agree to a large extent, since stars are paid to praise products they may not use, although some endorsements are genuine.

To begin with, celebrity endorsements can mislead because stars are paid to praise products they may not use. Fans trust the personality and assume that the recommendation is genuine, so claims about health or beauty may influence them without evidence. A footballer who promotes an energy drink, for example, probably does not consume it before matches, and a singer who recommends a face cream may use very different products at home. Contracts often specify what the star must say, and scripts are written by advertising agencies. Some celebrities promote financial products or supplements without understanding them, and followers have lost money or suffered health problems after trusting these messages.

Furthermore, endorsements exploit emotion and not reason. The product becomes attractive because of the fame of the person, not because of its quality, and this encourages purchases that people might otherwise avoid. However, not every endorsement is dishonest. Some stars choose brands that match their values and use them in real life, and a few donate their fees to charity. Transparency rules protect consumers. Laws should require stars to declare clearly when they are paid, ban claims that cannot be proved and punish false statements, and regulators can fine those who break the rules. Viewers should also remember that advertising aims to sell, and they should compare products independently.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that celebrity endorsements are misleading, but stricter transparency can reduce the problem.

essays.question: Many people think that online forums spread misinformation. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Questions about health, politics and technology are answered in seconds on online forums, and many people think that online forums spread misinformation. I agree to some extent, since posts are unchecked, although many forums also share expert help.

To begin with, online forums can spread misinformation because posts are unchecked. Anyone can post opinions as facts, and popular replies are not necessarily accurate. A user who asks about a medical symptom, for example, may receive a dozen confident answers from strangers with no training, and some of the advice may be dangerous. People often trust a reply simply because many others agree, and false claims that are repeated can start to look true. Anonymous accounts feel no responsibility for what they write, and some deliberately spread rumours or promote products. Because discussions move quickly, corrections are often buried and the original mistake spreads.

However, forums also have positive aspects. Moderators, expert members and links to sources correct many errors, and communities for professionals, such as programmers or doctors, often provide high-quality advice. A beginner who posts a computer problem, for example, can receive a precise solution from an expert within minutes. Forums are also a place where people can compare experiences, which is valuable when official information is limited. Users must verify claims. They should check whether a reply cites reliable sources, compare several opinions and consult professionals before acting on advice about health or money. Forum owners can improve quality through clear rules, active moderation and tools that highlight verified experts.

In conclusion, I agree to some extent that online forums spread misinformation, but careful use and good moderation can reduce the risk.

essays.question: Discuss the role of local media in small communities.

versions.text:
In a village or a small town, the weekly newspaper, the local radio station and the community website often provide the only news about what happens nearby, and this essay will discuss the role of local media in small communities, focusing on information and community identity.

To begin with, local media informs small communities about issues that national outlets ignore. A local paper or station reports council decisions, school events and local business, and holds officials to account. A resident who reads that the council plans to close a library, for example, can attend the meeting and protest before the decision is final. National channels rarely cover road repairs, planning applications or a missing pet, yet these affect everyday life. Local reporters know the area and can question mayors and officials, which makes corruption and waste harder to hide. Advertising in local media also helps small shops and farms to reach customers close by.

Furthermore, local media strengthens community identity. It celebrates local sports teams, festivals and achievements, gives space to residents' opinions and helps newcomers to feel at home. A radio programme in which elderly villagers tell stories about the past, for example, preserves memories and dialects that would otherwise be lost. In emergencies such as floods or snow, local stations provide immediate and relevant advice. However, falling advertising revenue and competition from online platforms make it hard for many small outlets to survive. Support from councils, donations from readers and partnerships with schools can keep them alive. When local media thrives, communities remain informed and connected.

In conclusion, local media plays an essential role in small communities by providing relevant news, holding authorities to account and strengthening a shared identity.

essays.question: Many people think that celebrity culture encourages materialism. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Magazines, television and social media fill daily life with pictures of famous people in expensive clothes, cars and houses, and many people think that celebrity culture encourages materialism. I agree with this view, since it presents luxury as the measure of success, although some celebrities live modestly.

To begin with, celebrity culture encourages materialism by presenting luxury as the measure of success. Constant images of designer clothes, cars and mansions make ordinary people feel that happiness depends on possessions. A young fan who sees her favourite singer buy a new handbag every week, for example, may start to believe that she needs the same brand in order to fit in. Programmes that show the homes and holidays of the rich make wealth appear normal and desirable, and advertisers use stars to sell products to millions of followers. Surveys suggest that young people who follow celebrity news closely place more importance on money and appearance and are more likely to run into debt.

However, not all celebrities encourage materialism. Some live modestly, give much of their income to charity or campaign for causes such as the environment and education, which shows that fame can serve other values. A footballer who funds a hospital instead of buying a fifth car, for example, sets a very different example. The influence also depends on the viewer, since families and schools can teach that character, effort and kindness matter more than possessions. Young people need alternative role models. Media can help by giving more attention to scientists, teachers, doctors and community leaders, whose achievements are based on knowledge and service and not on display.

In conclusion, I agree that celebrity culture encourages materialism, but its effect can be reduced by promoting different role models and values.

plan.think: Mở bài nêu hình ảnh người nổi tiếng xa hoa; agree.

essays.question: Many feel that advertising creates unrealistic expectations. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Advertisements show flawless models, spotless kitchens and products that promise happiness, and many feel that advertising creates unrealistic expectations. I agree with this view, since it presents edited images and exaggerated promises, although some adverts are honest.

To begin with, advertising creates unrealistic expectations of appearance and lifestyle. Edited models, perfect homes and promises of instant results make ordinary bodies and lives look inadequate. A woman who sees a skin cream advertised by a model with no visible pores, for example, may believe that the product will give her the same appearance, although the picture was altered by software and the model wears heavy make-up. Slimming products promise rapid weight loss without effort, and car adverts present empty roads and happy families, which do not match real traffic and daily stress. People who compare themselves with these images feel dissatisfied with their looks, homes and incomes, and they may buy more products in an attempt to close the gap.

Furthermore, unrealistic expectations can damage wellbeing, especially among teenagers who are still forming their self-image. Research links exposure to idealised bodies with low self-esteem and eating disorders. However, not all advertising is dishonest, and some campaigns now show diverse body types and real people. Honest labelling and diverse images reduce the harm. Laws can require clear notices when photographs have been retouched and ban claims that cannot be proved, while schools should teach students how images are produced. Consumers also have a role in treating advertisements with healthy scepticism.

In conclusion, I agree that advertising creates unrealistic expectations, but regulation and media education can limit its effects.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: quảng cáo tạo kỳ vọng phi thực tế — agree

plan.think: Mở bài nêu người mẫu hoàn hảo, bếp sạch tinh tươm; agree.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on celebrity culture? Use examples.

versions.text:
Famous actors, athletes and singers occupy magazines and screens in many nations, and this essay will discuss the benefits for a country that focuses on celebrity culture, using examples such as South Korea and the United States.

To begin with, a country with a strong celebrity culture gains tourism, cultural influence and fundraising power. Famous actors, athletes and musicians attract visitors and promote the nation abroad. South Korea, for example, has used its pop groups and television dramas to create worldwide interest in its language, food and fashion, and millions of tourists visit locations from their favourite programmes. Such soft power helps exports of cosmetics, electronics and cars, and it improves the country's image. Celebrity athletes can also inspire national pride during international competitions and encourage young people to take up sport.

Furthermore, celebrity culture supports a large entertainment industry and charitable giving. Film studios, record companies, fashion houses and media outlets create jobs for performers, technicians and designers, and their products earn export income. When stars campaign for charities, they can raise large sums quickly, as with the concerts and appeals held after natural disasters. Famous people also draw attention to causes such as the environment, health and education. The disadvantages include materialism, pressure on privacy and unrealistic images, but good regulation and attention to role models can reduce them. A country that manages celebrity culture well gains economic benefits and international prestige, while giving its young people examples of talent and hard work.

In conclusion, a country that focuses on celebrity culture benefits through tourism, cultural influence, jobs and fundraising, although the downsides must be managed.

analysis.type_vi: A/D (benefits): văn hoá người nổi tiếng đối với quốc gia — Hàn Quốc, Mỹ

essays.question: Many feel that online influencers promote unhealthy lifestyles. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Videos of morning routines, extreme diets and expensive holidays attract millions of viewers, and many feel that online influencers promote unhealthy lifestyles. I agree to a large extent, since they are paid per click and rarely have medical training, although some influencers offer helpful ideas.

To begin with, some influencers promote unhealthy lifestyles by recommending extreme diets, supplements and constant spending. They are paid per click and rarely have medical training, so followers copy risky habits. A fitness influencer who claims that she lost ten kilos in two weeks by drinking only juice, for example, may persuade young viewers to starve themselves, and some of the supplements that she promotes have never been tested. Others encourage heavy drinking, unhealthy snacks or gambling, because sponsors pay for these messages. Pictures of perfect bodies and luxurious lives create pressure to look and spend in the same way, which can lead to eating disorders and debt.

However, not all influencers harm their followers. Others share fitness and cooking ideas that help, such as simple home exercises, balanced recipes and advice about sleep or mental health. A chef who shows how to prepare cheap, healthy meals, for example, can improve the diet of thousands of families. Many influencers also raise awareness of illnesses and encourage medical check-ups. Disclosure rules and critical viewers limit the harm. Laws should require influencers to state when they are paid and to avoid health claims that cannot be proved, platforms can remove dangerous content, and parents and schools should teach young people to question what they see and to seek advice from qualified professionals.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that online influencers promote unhealthy lifestyles, but regulation and media literacy can reduce the risks.

essays.question: Many people think that exploitative behaviour on social media is harmful. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Some users film strangers in distress, post children in humiliating situations or invent emotional stories in order to get attention, and many people think that exploitative behaviour on social media is harmful. I agree with this view, since it turns the suffering or trust of others into profit.

To begin with, exploitative behaviour on social media harms victims by turning their suffering or trust into profit. Some users film children or accidents for views, scammers use fake charities, and platforms reward shocking content. A parent who films a small child crying in order to produce a funny video, for example, may earn money, but the child is deprived of privacy and may be embarrassed for years when classmates find the clip. People who record an accident instead of helping gain attention at the expense of the victims and their families. Scam accounts that appeal for money for sick children cause donors to lose money and harm genuine charities. Vulnerable people, including the elderly and the lonely, are often targeted by fraudsters who pretend to be friends or partners.

Furthermore, such behaviour affects society by making cruelty and deception normal. Users learn that shocking or dishonest content earns rewards, which encourages more of it. However, not all attention-seeking is exploitative, and many creators earn a living honestly. Rules, reporting tools and public pressure are needed to limit the harm. Governments should protect children by regulating the use of minors in online content, platforms should remove scams and offer easy reporting systems, and users should refuse to share or reward exploitative posts. Education can also help people to recognise warning signs of fraud.

In conclusion, I agree that exploitative behaviour on social media is harmful, and it requires action by platforms, governments and users.

essays.question: To what extent do you agree or disagree that traditional newspapers will disappear?

versions.text:
Fewer people buy printed newspapers each year, and the question is to what extent traditional newspapers will disappear. I agree to a limited extent, since print newspapers will shrink and may largely disappear, but quality journalism will continue online.

To begin with, print newspapers are in long-term decline. Readers and advertisers have moved to digital platforms, making printing expensive. A local newspaper that once sold twenty thousand copies a day, for example, may now sell only a few thousand, and it cannot cover the cost of paper, ink and delivery. Young people get news from their phones and rarely buy a paper, and classified advertisements, which used to produce large profits, have moved to websites. Many titles have closed or merged, and some have stopped printing on weekdays. If this trend continues, print editions may become rare luxury items.

However, journalism itself will not disappear, and a number of newspapers are adapting successfully. Many titles keep subscribers and move to paid websites and apps, which give them a direct relationship with readers and allow them to produce investigative reporting. Some readers also value the paper format for long articles, for the feel of a weekend edition and for relaxing away from screens. A newspaper that publishes a weekly printed magazine with in-depth essays, for example, can still attract loyal customers. The medium will therefore change while news survives. Society needs trained reporters to check facts and to question those in power, and readers who recognise this value are willing to pay for it.

In conclusion, traditional printed newspapers will probably shrink greatly, but journalism will continue in digital form, so I agree only to a limited extent that newspapers will disappear.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for their media consumption, or should society/government regulate content? Discuss.

versions.text:
Television, streaming services and social networks offer unlimited content, and opinions differ on whether individuals should be responsible for their media consumption or whether society and government should regulate content. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of individual responsibility argue that adults can choose what to watch and learn to judge sources. A person who dislikes violent films can simply avoid them, and viewers can compare several news outlets to find reliable information. Parents can set rules at home, use filters and talk to children about what they see, and schools can teach media literacy. Freedom of choice is also a basic principle, and regulation by officials risks restricting opinions and art that they dislike. People who learn to question what they read become more independent and less likely to be manipulated.

On the other hand, supporters of regulation point out that children and vulnerable people need protection from harmful content, which only rules and platform duties can provide. Young children cannot judge a violent or sexual video, and adults may be misled by deliberate disinformation. A child who stumbles upon extreme material through an automatic recommendation, for example, has not made a choice at all. Media companies profit from attention, and without limits they may promote sensational content. Governments can require age checks, remove illegal material, demand transparency about algorithms and punish serious abuse. Media consumption needs both responsible users and sensible rules.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that responsibility should be shared: individuals and families should make informed choices, while society regulates clearly harmful material and protects children.

essays.question: Some people say that commercial advertising on public transport should be banned. Do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Posters on the sides of buses and in metro carriages are seen by millions of passengers, and some people say that commercial advertising on public transport should be banned. I disagree, since advertising raises money to keep fares low, although content rules are needed.

To begin with, advertising on public transport raises money to keep fares low. Operators earn substantial income from adverts, which helps to pay for services. A city whose buses carry posters, for example, may collect millions each year, which can be used to maintain vehicles, lower ticket prices or run extra services at night. If advertising were banned, the revenue would have to come from higher fares or from taxpayers, which means that poorer passengers would pay more or that other public services would be cut. Adverts on trains and stations also help local businesses and event organisers to reach a large audience cheaply, and they can brighten otherwise dull spaces with colour and creativity.

However, passengers cannot avoid advertisements, and some images are offensive or unhealthy. Travellers who stand in a carriage are forced to look at posters for alcohol, junk food or unrealistic body images, and parents of young children may object. Rather than a total ban, strict content rules would be a better answer. Authorities can prohibit adverts that are sexist, violent or misleading, restrict promotion of tobacco, alcohol and unhealthy food on public property, and limit the number of adverts in each vehicle. Regulated advertising balances revenue and public interest, and it respects both passengers and operators.

In conclusion, I disagree that commercial advertising on public transport should be banned, but it should be regulated carefully.

essays.question: Many feel that documentary films are more educational than fictional films. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Schools, museums and television channels all use films to teach, and many people feel that documentary films are more educational than fictional films. I agree to a large extent, since documentaries present facts and evidence about real subjects, although fiction can teach in other ways.

To begin with, documentaries are usually more directly educational. They present facts, interviews and evidence about real subjects, such as wildlife, wars or scientific discoveries. A student who watches a documentary about the rainforest, for example, sees real animals, hears from biologists and learns how forests affect the climate, all within one hour. Maps, graphs and archive film make complex information clear, and the viewer can check the sources and continue reading afterwards. Teachers often use documentaries to supplement textbooks, because they bring distant places and events into the classroom. Because they aim to inform, they usually stay close to the truth and avoid the invented events and exaggerations that fiction often contains.

However, fiction can also teach important lessons. Stories build understanding of people and history through characters who move viewers, and they develop empathy by letting audiences see the world through other eyes. A film about a family during a war, for example, may help young people to understand suffering far better than a list of dates and numbers. Historical dramas can inspire interest in a period that leads viewers to further study. Both belong in education, but they serve different purposes: documentaries give knowledge and evidence, and fiction gives emotional insight. Teachers should combine them and encourage students to ask which parts are true and which are imagined.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that documentary films are more educational than fictional films, although fiction has its own value.

essays.question: Some believe that advertising to children should be tightly regulated. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Children see thousands of advertisements every year, and some believe that advertising to children should be tightly regulated. I agree to a large extent, since children cannot judge persuasion and need protection, although parents also have a role.

To begin with, advertising to children should be tightly regulated because they are unable to judge persuasion. Young children do not understand that adverts sell, so cartoon characters and games lead them to demand toys and sugary snacks. A boy who sees a famous footballer promoting a fizzy drink, for example, may believe that the drink will make him strong, and he will ask his parents for it repeatedly. Advertisers deliberately use bright colours, catchy songs and free gifts to attract children and to create brand loyalty at an early age. This pressure on parents, called pester power, causes family conflict and spending that families may not be able to afford, and it increases demand for unhealthy products.

However, regulation should be balanced and supported by other measures. Parents have an important responsibility to monitor what their children watch, to explain how advertising works and to say no. Schools can include media education in their lessons, and broadcasters can voluntarily follow codes of conduct. Some advertisements for books, sports equipment or educational products are beneficial, so a total ban may be unnecessary. Strict rules should nevertheless exist: governments can prohibit adverts for unhealthy foods during children's programmes, forbid the use of cartoon characters to sell harmful products, ban direct appeals to buy and check that websites and games do not hide promotions in entertainment. Effective enforcement with fines for violations is essential.

In conclusion, I agree that advertising to children should be tightly regulated, as long as parents and schools also help children to understand advertising.

essays.question: Many feel that influencer culture creates unrealistic lifestyles. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Followers see influencers on tropical beaches, in luxury hotels and in spotless homes, and many feel that influencer culture creates unrealistic lifestyles. I agree with this view, since sponsored, staged and edited content hides the effort and money behind it.

To begin with, influencer culture creates unrealistic lifestyles by showing sponsored, staged and edited versions of life. Free gifts, paid trips and perfect scenes hide the effort and money behind them. A travel influencer who posts a photograph from a luxury resort, for example, may have received the stay free in return for promotion, and may have taken dozens of shots before choosing the one with perfect light. The viewer, who sees only the final picture, believes that the lifestyle is normal and affordable. Many influencers rent clothes, cars and even houses for filming, and some use filters that change their appearance. The constant stream of glamorous images makes ordinary routines look dull by comparison.

Furthermore, this affects followers. People feel that their own lives are not good enough, and some spend money or borrow to keep up with what they see. Young people, who spend hours on these platforms, are particularly vulnerable, and studies connect heavy use with anxiety and low self-confidence. However, not every influencer is dishonest, and some share real struggles and everyday life. Honest disclosure and critical viewing reduce the harm. Rules can require influencers to label paid partnerships and edited images, and platforms can promote creators who show realistic content. Parents and teachers should discuss with young people how these images are produced and encourage them to measure their lives by their own values.

In conclusion, I agree that influencer culture creates unrealistic lifestyles, but transparency and media education can reduce its effects.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: văn hoá người ảnh hưởng tạo lối sống phi thực tế — agree

plan.think: Mở bài nêu người ảnh hưởng ở bãi biển nhiệt đới, khách sạn sang; agree.

Cho thấy phiên bản được tài trợ, dàn dựng, chỉnh sửa: quà tặng, chuyến đi trả tiền, cảnh hoàn hảo che nỗ lực, tiền; ví dụ người ảnh hưởng du lịch đăng ảnh khu nghỉ sang có thể được ở miễn phí đổi quảng bá, chụp hàng chục kiểu mới chọn ánh sáng hoàn hảo; người xem tin bình thường, mua nổi; thuê quần áo, xe, nhà để quay; bộ lọc; dòng ảnh quyến rũ làm đời thường nhàm.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for reporting misinformation, or should society/government act? Discuss.

versions.text:
False health advice, doctored photographs and invented political stories circulate widely, and opinions differ on whether individuals should be responsible for reporting misinformation or whether society and government should act. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of individual responsibility argue that ordinary users are best placed to notice and report false posts. Users spot false posts quickly and can report them. A teacher who sees a fake claim about a vaccine in a parents' group, for example, can flag it and explain the facts before it spreads, and thousands of such reports can help platforms to find harmful material. People who check a source before sharing, and who correct friends politely, make it more difficult for rumours to travel. Since misinformation spreads through personal networks, personal habits are important, and a population that learns to think critically is the strongest defence.

On the other hand, advocates of action by society and government point out that individuals lack the power to remove false posts, to check facts at scale or to punish deliberate spreaders. Individuals can flag misinformation but platforms and governments must act on it. Companies decide how algorithms work and can slow the spread of false stories, fact-checking organisations need funding, and laws can penalise organised campaigns that aim to deceive voters. A single user cannot stop a network of fake accounts, for example, that floods a platform with false claims. Without official action, reports are often ignored.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that responsibility is shared: individuals should check and report misleading content, while platforms and governments must act on reports and enforce clear rules against deliberate disinformation.
